message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is not legal advice; if you have a specific dispute, consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months for an unfurnished unit.
• The deposit must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (e.g., unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear).
• Landlords must provide a written itemized statement of deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease, move‑in inspection sheet, and any receipts for repairs.
• Request the deposit return in writing and keep a copy. | | **Habitability / Repairs** | • Texas Property Code §92.001 requires landlords to maintain premises in a safe, sanitary condition and to repair major defects.
• Tenants may withhold rent only if the landlord fails to make necessary repairs after notice. | • Give written notice of needed repairs and allow reasonable time for completion.
• If repairs are not made, you may file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or pursue a “repair‑and‑deduct” action in small‑claims court. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For month‑to‑month leases: 30‑day written notice to terminate.
• For fixed‑term leases: the lease itself governs termination; otherwise, a 30‑day notice is required if the lease ends. | • Always provide notice in writing (email or certified mail) and keep proof of delivery. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas Property Code §92.005: serve a 3‑day notice for non‑payment of rent, a 30‑day notice for lease violations, or a 60‑day notice for lease termination (unless the lease specifies otherwise).
• After the notice period, the landlord files a lawsuit in district court. | • Respond promptly to notices; negotiate payment plans if possible.
• If you believe the eviction is unlawful, file a counter‑claim in the same lawsuit. | | **Privacy / Entry** | • Landlords must give at least 24 hours’ written notice before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of all entries; if you suspect unlawful entry, report it to the local police or TDHCA. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the Texas Fair Housing Act, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes. | • Report discriminatory practices to the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR). | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has no statewide rent‑control laws; rent increases are governed by the lease agreement. | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses; if the increase is unreasonable, you may negotiate or seek mediation. | | **Lease Renewal & Rent Increases** | • For month‑to‑month tenants, landlords must give 30‑day notice before raising rent. | • Negotiate a fixed‑rate renewal if you plan to stay long term. | | **Utilities & Services** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. If the landlord provides essential services (heat, hot water), they must maintain them. | • Keep records of utility payments and any service interruptions. | | **Legal Remedies** | • Small‑claims court (up to $20,000) for disputes over deposits, damages, or unpaid rent.
• Mediation services offered by the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs. | • File claims promptly; keep all documentation (photos, receipts, correspondence). | ### Where to Get Help | Resource | What It Offers | How to Contact | |----------|----------------|----------------| | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** | Consumer complaints, landlord‑tenant mediation, enforcement of housing codes. | Phone: 1‑800‑TRUST‑TX (1‑800‑872‑7848) or online portal. | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR)** | Complaint filing for discrimination. | Phone: 1‑800‑TRUST‑TX (1‑800‑872‑7848) or online. | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | Legal clinics, workshops, advocacy. | Search “tenant rights Texas” + city name. | | **Small‑Claims Court** | Resolve disputes over deposits, damages, unpaid rent. | File at your county district court clerk’s office. | --- #### Quick Checklist Before Moving Out 1. **Review Lease** – Note any move‑out inspection requirements or deposit deductions. 2. **Document Condition** – Take photos/video of each room, appliances, and any existing damage. 3. **Provide Written Notice** – Send a 30‑day notice (or as required by lease). 4. **Schedule Inspection** – Arrange a walk‑through with the landlord. 5. **Keep Records** – Save copies of all correspondence, receipts, and the move‑out inspection sheet. If you encounter a situation that isn’t covered here or need personalized guidance, consider contacting a local attorney or a tenant‑rights nonprofit.
message.reasoning: The user asks: "What are my rights as a tenant in the state of Texas?" They want information about tenant rights. We can provide general info. There's no request for generating a contract. So we don't need to call the function. Just answer. Provide overview: security deposit, habitability, notice, eviction, etc. Also mention resources. Provide citations? We can give a concise but thorough answer.
